questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with pain around the lower part of his ear. He reports difficulty chewing food and is unable to fully close his eyes. On physical examination, there is noticeable swelling beneath his ear. Which nerve is most likely compromised in this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Facial nerve

 

  • The patient's symptoms — pain near the ear lobule, difficulty eating (suggesting impaired muscles of mastication or facial expression), and inability to close the eyes completely — along with swelling below the ear, point toward involvement of the facial nerve. 
  • The facial nerve innervates muscles of facial expression, including those responsible for eye closure and movements of the mouth. 
  • Swelling below the ear could indicate parotid gland involvement or inflammation affecting the facial nerve as it passes through or near the gland.
  • Dysfunction leads to facial muscle weakness, difficulty closing the eye, and problems with facial expressions, including eating.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Auriculotemporal nerve: This nerve primarily provides sensation to parts of the ear and temporal region but does not control muscles responsible for eye closure or facial expressions.

 

Option C. Vagus nerve: The vagus nerve innervates structures in the neck, thorax, and abdomen and is not involved in facial muscle movement or sensation around the ear lobule.

 

Option D. Great auricular nerve: This nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin over the parotid region and ear but does not affect facial muscle function or eye closure.

 

Educational objective:


The facial nerve controls muscles of facial expression, including eyelid closure and mouth movements; swelling near the ear causing inability to close the eye and difficulty eating suggests facial nerve involvement.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the anatomical connection made by Sharpey’s fibers?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Periosteum to bone
 

  • Sharpey’s fibers are collagenous fibers that anchor the periosteum firmly to the underlying bone. 
  • They penetrate the outer layers of the bone, providing mechanical stability and allowing for effective transfer of forces. 
  • This connection is crucial for maintaining the integrity of the periosteal attachment and facilitating bone remodeling and repair.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Periosteum to synovial membrane: The synovial membrane lines the joint cavity and does not directly connect to the periosteum via Sharpey’s fibers.

 

Option B. Enamel to dentin: This junction is the dentino-enamel junction, which is unrelated to Sharpey’s fibers.

 

Option D. Joint capsule to periosteum: While the joint capsule attaches near the periosteum, Sharpey’s fibers specifically connect the periosteum to bone, not the capsule to the periosteum.

 

Educational Objective:


Sharpey’s fibers connect the periosteum to the underlying bone, securing the periosteal layer and aiding in the mechanical stability of bone.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is being evaluated for erectile dysfunction. Understanding the arterial supply to the penis is essential in managing his condition. Which artery is primarily responsible for giving rise to the helicine arteries that facilitate penile erection?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Deep artery of the penis

 

  • The helicine arteries, which are responsible for supplying blood to the erectile tissue of the corpora cavernosa, arise from the deep artery of the penis. 
  • These arteries have a tortuous course and dilate during erection, allowing increased blood flow into the cavernous spaces, leading to penile tumescence. 
  • The deep artery plays a vital role in the vascular mechanism of erection.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Dorsal artery of the penis: Supplies the skin, glans, and the penile fascia but does not give rise to the helicine arteries involved in erection.

 

Option C. Bulbourethral artery: Primarily supplies the bulb and the urethra, not the erectile tissue.

 

Option D. Perineal artery: Supplies the muscles and skin of the perineum but is not involved in the arterial supply of the helicine arteries.

 

Educational Objective:


The deep artery of the penis gives rise to the helicine arteries, which are critical for delivering blood into the corpora cavernosa and enabling penile erection.

questions.stem: During a surgical procedure involving ligation of the common hepatic artery, which of the following arterial supplies is most likely to be compromised as a result?

options.label: A
options.text: Right gastroepiploic and short gastric vessels

options.label: B
options.text: Right gastric and right gastroepiploic artery

options.label: C
options.text: Right gastric and short gastric vessels

options.label: D
options.text: Right gastric and left gastric artery

questions.answerText: Right gastric and right gastroepiploic artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Right gastric and right gastroepiploic artery
 

  • The common hepatic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk, gives rise to several important branches including the right gastric artery and the gastroduodenal artery, which in turn gives rise to the right gastroepiploic artery. 
  • Therefore, ligation of the common hepatic artery will impair blood flow through both the right gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries, as they originate downstream of this vessel. 
  • This disruption can compromise blood supply to portions of the stomach that rely on these arteries.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Right gastroepiploic and short gastric vessels: The short gastric vessels arise from the splenic artery, not the common hepatic artery, so they are unaffected by its ligation.

 

Option C. Right gastric and short gastric vessels: The short gastric vessels (from the splenic artery) remain patent after common hepatic artery ligation.

 

Option D. Right gastric and left gastric artery: The left gastric artery is a direct branch from the celiac trunk and not affected by ligation of the common hepatic artery.

 

Educational Objective:


Ligation of the common hepatic artery impairs blood flow through its distal branches, most notably the right gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries, affecting gastric perfusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following anatomical structures is not classified as a synovial joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Symphysis pubis

 

  • The symphysis pubis is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), not a synovial joint. 
  • It consists of fibrocartilage between the pubic bones and allows only limited movement, mainly for shock absorption and support. 
  • It lacks a synovial cavity and synovial membrane, which are defining features of synovial joints.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Radiocarpal joint: This is a true synovial joint, specifically an ellipsoid type, formed between the distal radius and carpal bones, allowing flexion, extension, and circumduction.

 

Option C. Costotransverse joint: A plane type of synovial joint between the tubercle of a rib and the transverse process of its corresponding vertebra.

 

Option D. Costovertebral joint: Also a synovial joint, between the head of the rib and the body of the thoracic vertebrae, permitting slight gliding movements.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The symphysis pubis is a fibrocartilaginous joint, not a synovial joint; it lacks a synovial cavity and permits only limited movement.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old male presents to the emergency department with acute hand pain and swelling after striking a hard surface with a closed fist. On examination, there is tenderness over the dorsum of the hand and mild deformity without obvious dislocation. Based on this mechanism of injury, which of the following bones is most likely fractured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Metacarpals

 

  • Punching a wall or similar object with a closed fist commonly results in fractures of the metacarpal bones, particularly the fifth metacarpal—a classic injury pattern known as a boxer’s fracture. 
  • This occurs due to the axial load transmitted through the clenched hand during impact. 
  • Patients often present with pain, swelling, and possible rotational deformity of the affected digit. 
  • It is most common in young males following trauma associated with anger or impulsivity.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hamate: Although the hamate is a carpal bone that can be fractured in activities involving gripping (e.g., golf, baseball), it is not the most likely site in the setting of a direct punching injury.

 

Option B. Phalanges: Phalangeal fractures typically occur due to direct trauma to the fingers, not from punching a wall with a clenched fist.

 

Option D. Distal radius: This bone is more commonly fractured in falls on an outstretched hand, especially in elderly patients, not from punching injuries.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Metacarpal fractures, particularly of the fifth metacarpal, are the most common hand injuries following a closed-fist impact, such as punching a wall.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with progressive vision loss. Neuroimaging reveals compression of the optic chiasma by an adjacent saccular aneurysm. Which of the following arteries is most commonly associated with this pattern of compression?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anterior communicating artery

 

  • The anterior communicating artery is the most common site of intracranial aneurysms that compress the optic chiasma, leading to visual disturbances, particularly bitemporal hemianopia. 
  • This artery connects the two anterior cerebral arteries and lies directly superior to the optic chiasma. 
  • Aneurysmal dilation at this location can press on the chiasma, which houses the crossing fibers from the nasal retinae—resulting in characteristic visual field deficits.

 

 

Other Options:


Option B. Middle cerebral artery: While this artery is commonly involved in ischemic strokes and aneurysms, it lies laterally in the Sylvian fissure and does not commonly cause optic chiasma compression.


Option C. Anterior cerebral artery: This vessel lies anterior to the optic chiasma but aneurysms here are less likely to directly compress the chiasma compared to its communicating branch.


Option D. Anterior choroidal artery: This is a small branch of the internal carotid artery that supplies the optic tract and posterior limb of the internal capsule. Aneurysms here can affect the optic tract, not the optic chiasma.

 

Educational objective:


Aneurysms of the anterior communicating artery are the most common vascular lesions that compress the optic chiasma, leading to visual field defects.

questions.stemHtml: What is the most accurate identification of the microscopic appearance of the tissue given below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Skin

 

  • The histological slide shows classic features of skin, including:
    • A stratified squamous keratinized epithelium (epidermis),
    • Numerous hair follicles extending deep into the dermis,
    • Associated sebaceous glands and sweat glands,
    • Dense irregular connective tissue forming the dermis and hypodermis.
  • These features are hallmark components of integumentary tissue, confirming that the slide represents skin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lymph node: Lymph nodes show a capsule, cortex, and medulla with lymphoid follicles—not stratified squamous epithelium or hair follicles.

 

Option C. Cartilage: Cartilage histology includes chondrocytes in lacunae and an extracellular matrix, without skin appendages like hair follicles or glands.

 

Option D. Collagen: Collagen is a fibrous protein, not a tissue type. Although it is present in skin, it does not alone represent a tissue with hair follicles and glands.

 

Educational Objective:


Histological identification of skin involves recognizing features such as stratified squamous epithelium, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands, distinguishing it from other tissues like lymph nodes or cartilage.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the right coronary artery is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Right conus artery is its first branch

options.label: B
options.text: It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch

options.label: C
options.text: Its diameter is less than the left coronary artery

options.label: D
options.text: It arises from the anterior aortic sinus

questions.answerText: It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch

 

  • The right coronary artery (RCA) originates from the anterior aortic sinus (also called the right coronary sinus).
  • Its first branch is typically the right conus artery, which supplies the conus arteriosus (infundibulum) of the right ventricle.
  • Compared to the left coronary artery (LCA), the RCA generally has a smaller diameter, as the LCA divides early into major branches (LAD and circumflex), each covering a large myocardial territory.
  • The circumflex artery, however, is a branch of the LCA, not the RCA.
  • Therefore, option B is incorrect and is the correct answer to the "except" question.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Right conus artery is its first branch: Correct. This is usually the first branch of the RCA.

 

Option C. Its diameter is less than the left coronary artery: Correct. The LCA typically has a larger diameter due to its extensive perfusion area.

 

Option D. It arises from the anterior aortic sinus: Correct. The RCA originates from the anterior (right) aortic sinus of the ascending aorta.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The circumflex coronary artery arises from the left coronary artery, not the right; all other features listed are true of the right coronary artery.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents after a forearm injury sustained while working with machinery. During examination, he is asked to make a fist, but the index and middle fingers remain partially extended, while the ring and little fingers flex normally. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Median nerve

 

  • Injury to the median nerve leads to an inability to flex the first three digits due to dysfunction of the:
    • Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS): affects all fingers
    • Lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus (FDP): affects digits 2 and 3
    • Thenar muscles: particularly opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, and flexor pollicis brevis
  • This results in the “hand of benediction” when the patient attempts to make a fist—the index and middle fingers remain extended, while digits 4 and 5 (innervated by the ulnar nerve) flex normally. This pattern suggests an injury to the median nerve, typically at or above the elbow.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Musculocutaneous nerve: Innervates biceps, brachialis, and coracobrachialis, contributing to forearm flexion, not finger flexion. Its injury causes weak elbow flexion, not a fist-closing deficit.

 

Option B. Ulnar nerve: Injury leads to problems with flexion of digits 4 and 5 and claw hand deformity, not with digits 2 and 3. The hand of benediction would not be seen.

 

Option D. Radial nerve: Radial nerve controls wrist and finger extension. Injury causes wrist drop, not an inability to flex the index and middle fingers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Inability to flex the index and middle fingers when attempting to make a fist—resulting in a "hand of benediction"—is characteristic of a median nerve injury affecting the flexor digitorum muscles and thenar muscles. This typically occurs with proximal forearm trauma.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following key features is most consistent with the histological findings seen in the provided image?

options.label: D
options.text: Presence of white and red pulp

questions.answerText: Presence of white and red pulp
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Presence of white and red pulp

 

  • The histological image presented demonstrates a distinct architectural pattern typical of splenic tissue. The spleen is characterized by two main components:
    • White pulp, which consists of lymphoid tissue arranged around central arterioles (periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths) and lymphoid follicles.
    • Red pulp, which is rich in blood-filled sinusoids and splenic cords (cords of Billroth) responsible for filtering blood and removing old or damaged erythrocytes.
  • This combination produces alternating dark (white pulp) and light (red pulp) areas under hematoxylin and eosin staining. The image clearly shows this arrangement, confirming that the organ in question is the spleen, and the most prominent feature is the presence of white and red pulp.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lymphoid follicle: While white pulp of the spleen does include lymphoid follicles, the presence of only lymphoid follicles is not sufficient to define the overall architecture of the spleen. This option fails to capture the essential dual composition (white and red pulp) that characterizes splenic histology. Thus, this answer is incomplete and not the most prominent feature shown in the image.

 

Option B. Central vein and Hepatocytes: These features are characteristic of liver histology, not the spleen. In liver tissue, hepatocytes are arranged around a central vein in hepatic lobules. These features are absent in the provided histological image and do not explain the observed architecture.

 

Option C. Brunner’s glands: Brunner’s glands are located in the submucosa of the duodenum and secrete alkaline mucus to neutralize gastric acid. Histologically, they appear as mucin-secreting glands. The current image does not show glandular structures in submucosa or any duodenal histological patterns, making this choice irrelevant.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The spleen is histologically identified by its unique dual architecture composed of white pulp (lymphoid tissue) and red pulp (vascular sinusoids and splenic cords). 
  • Recognizing this pattern is crucial for differentiating splenic tissue from other abdominal organs.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes) following blunt trauma to the scalp. Imaging confirms a basilar skull fracture, and the physical exam shows bilateral blood pooling around the eyes without direct trauma to the orbits. The blood has tracked anteriorly under the scalp. Which anatomical layer is most responsible for allowing this spread of blood from the scalp to the periorbital region?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Loose areolar layer

 

  • The loose areolar tissue layer of the scalp is known as the "danger area of the scalp" because:
    • It is a potential space between the aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) and the periosteum (pericranium).
    • This layer allows for easy spread of infection or blood through emissary veins, which can track into intracranial structures.
    • Following head trauma, blood from injured vessels in the scalp or underlying bone can collect here and spread anteriorly, causing periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes).
  • This explains how blood migrates from the site of trauma on the scalp to the eyelids without orbital injury.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aponeurotic layer: Also called the galea aponeurotica, it connects the frontalis and occipitalis muscles but is not responsible for fluid spread. It lies just superficial to the loose areolar layer.

 

Option C. Periosteum (Pericranium): It is the deepest layer of the scalp, tightly adherent to the skull bones, and does not allow tracking of fluid or blood.

 

Option D. Connective tissue layer: Refers to the dense connective tissue just beneath the skin. It contains blood vessels but is too dense to permit spread of blood to other regions, such as the periorbital area.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The loose areolar layer of the scalp, known as the "danger zone," allows for the spread of blood or infection, including tracking of blood to the periorbital region following scalp trauma, leading to raccoon eyes or periorbital ecchymosis.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with complaints of dragging his foot while walking. He notes that he often trips over his toes. Neurological examination reveals difficulty dorsiflexing the foot at the ankle joint, and a high-stepping gait is observed. Which of the following nerves is most likely affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Deep Peroneal (Fibular) Nerve

 

  • The patient's complaint of dragging the foot, especially with difficulty in dorsiflexion, indicates a condition commonly referred to as foot drop. The most specific cause of foot drop is injury or dysfunction of the:
  • Deep peroneal (fibular) nerve, which innervates:
    • Tibialis anterior (primary dorsiflexor)
    • Extensor hallucis longus
    • Extensor digitorum longus

 

Damage to this nerve leads to inability to dorsiflex the foot, resulting in foot drop and a compensatory high-stepping gait to avoid toe dragging.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sciatic Nerve: While the sciatic nerve gives rise to the common peroneal nerve, isolated dorsiflexion weakness without other signs (e.g., hamstring weakness or complete foot involvement) suggests a more distal lesion, specifically of the deep peroneal nerve.

 

Option C. Tibial Nerve: Innervates plantarflexors of the foot and the posterior compartment. Lesions here cause difficulty with plantarflexion, not dorsiflexion.

 

Option D. Sural Nerve: A sensory nerve supplying the posterolateral leg and lateral foot. It has no motor function, so it cannot cause foot drop.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Foot drop (inability to dorsiflex the foot) is most commonly due to injury to the deep peroneal (fibular) nerve, which innervates the muscles responsible for ankle dorsiflexion. 
  • This condition results in a high-stepping gait to compensate for the dragging foot.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is evaluated for persistent neck stiffness. During examination, the physician notes restricted flexion-extension (“nodding”) and rotation (“shaking”) movements of the head. Which of the following joint pairs are primarily responsible for these actions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Atlanto-axial joint and atlanto-occipital joint

 

  • Movements of the head occur primarily at two specialized upper cervical joints:
  1. Atlanto-occipital joint (between the occipital condyles and the superior articular facets of the atlas, C1):
    • Responsible for flexion and extension of the head (e.g., "yes" movement or nodding).
  2. Atlanto-axial joint (between the atlas [C1] and the axis [C2]):
    • Responsible for rotation of the head (e.g., "no" movement or shaking).
    • Especially the median atlanto-axial joint, a pivot joint between the dens of C2 and the anterior arch of C1.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Sternoclavicular joint and costovertebral joint: These joints are involved in shoulder and thoracic movements, respectively. They play no role in head nodding or rotation.

 

Option C. Sacroiliac joint and hip joint: These joints are located in the pelvis and lower limbs and are unrelated to head or neck movement.

 

Option D. Glenohumeral joint and temporomandibular joint: The glenohumeral joint enables shoulder movement, while the TMJ controls jaw movement. Neither is involved in head nodding or shaking.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Flexion and extension ("nodding") of the head occurs at the atlanto-occipital joint, while rotation ("shaking") of the head occurs at the atlanto-axial joint. 
  • These specialized cervical joints are critical for upper neck mobility and head positioning.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the structures that pierces the clavipectoral fascia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thoracoacromial artery

 

  • The clavipectoral fascia (also called the costocoracoid membrane) is a deep fascia located between the pectoralis major and subclavius/pectoralis minor muscles. It is pierced by several important structures as they exit the axilla or pass into it, including:
    • Thoracoacromial artery: A branch of the axillary artery that emerges through the clavipectoral fascia to supply the pectoralis muscles, deltoid, and shoulder region.
    • Cephalic vein: Drains into the axillary vein through the fascia.
    • Lateral pectoral nerve: Also pierces this fascia to supply the pectoralis major.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Axillary nerve: Passes through the quadrangular space and innervates the deltoid and teres minor. It does not pierce the clavipectoral fascia.

 

Option C. Suprascapular artery: Arises from the thyrocervical trunk and courses over the superior border of the scapula. It is not anatomically associated with the clavipectoral fascia.

 

Option D. Long thoracic nerve: Arises from the roots of C5–C7 and travels on the lateral thoracic wall to supply the serratus anterior. It does not pierce the clavipectoral fascia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The thoracoacromial artery, along with the cephalic vein and lateral pectoral nerve, pierces the clavipectoral fascia to reach the pectoral and deltoid regions. Understanding these anatomical pathways is critical during axillary surgery and dissection.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man undergoes evaluation for suspected prostate cancer. During a digital rectal exam, the physician notes the close proximity of the rectal wall to the seminal vesicles. The inferior ends of the seminal vesicles are separated from the rectum by which of the following anatomical structures?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Rectovesical septum

 

  • The rectovesical septum (also known as Denonvilliers' fascia) is a fibrous connective tissue layer that lies between the rectum and the posterior surface of the prostate and seminal vesicles in males. It provides:
    • A surgical plane used during prostatectomy
    • A barrier between the seminal vesicles/prostate and the rectum
    • Protection of rectal structures during surgical interventions
  • Thus, the inferior ends of the seminal vesicles are separated from the rectum only by the rectovesical septum.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pubovesical ligament: Attaches the bladder to the pubic bone in females (and less significantly in males). It is not located between the seminal vesicles and rectum.

 

Option B. Puboprostatic ligament: Connects the prostate to the pubic bone. It supports the bladder and prostate anteriorly, not posteriorly.

 

Option D. Puborectalis muscle: Part of the levator ani muscle group, forming a sling around the anorectal junction to maintain fecal continence. It lies inferior to the level of the seminal vesicles and does not separate them from the rectum.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The rectovesical septum (Denonvilliers’ fascia) is the key structure that separates the seminal vesicles and prostate from the rectum and is an important anatomical landmark during pelvic surgery.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old patient who recently underwent surgery for varicose veins now presents with a complaint of sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot. Physical examination confirms diminished light touch sensation in that region, while motor function remains intact. Injury to which of the following nerves during the procedure is the most likely cause of this deficit?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Saphenous nerve

 

  • The saphenous nerve is a purely sensory branch of the femoral nerve, and it travels along the medial aspect of the thigh and leg. It accompanies the great saphenous vein, which is often involved in varicose vein surgery or vein stripping.
  • Injury to the saphenous nerve during these procedures can lead to sensory loss in the medial leg and medial side of the foot.
  • Since the saphenous nerve has no motor fibers, patients do not experience weakness, only sensory disturbances.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Superficial peroneal nerve: Provides sensation to the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot, not the medial side. It is also more lateral in course and not typically involved in varicose vein surgeries.

 

Option B. Deep peroneal nerve: Innervates muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg and provides sensory innervation only to the web space between the first and second toes. It does not supply the medial leg or foot.

 

Option D. Sural nerve: Supplies the posterolateral leg and lateral foot. Damage would cause lateral sensory loss, not medial.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The saphenous nerve runs in close proximity to the great saphenous vein and is at risk of injury during varicose vein surgery. 
  • Damage to this nerve results in sensory loss over the medial leg and foot, without motor involvement, due to its purely sensory function.

questions.stem: At which of the following vertebral levels does the formation of the portal vein occur?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) L1

 

  • The portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric vein (SMV) and the splenic vein, which occurs:
    • Posterior to the neck of the pancreas
    • At the level of the L1 vertebra, also known as the transpyloric plane
  • This location is clinically significant in liver disease, pancreatic pathology, and during surgical procedures involving portal circulation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. T12: This level corresponds more closely to the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm where the aorta enters the abdomen, not the site of portal vein formation.

 

Option C. L2: Lies below the actual level of portal vein formation. While some major vessels course here, it is not the formation site.

 

Option D. L3:  Farther inferior to the portal vein origin, closer to where the inferior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein in some anatomical variations.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The portal vein is formed at the L1 vertebral level, posterior to the neck of the pancreas, by the convergence of the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein—a critical anatomical and clinical landmark.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old construction worker falls from a ladder and sustains a midshaft fracture of the humerus. On examination, he exhibits wrist drop and diminished sensation over the posterior aspect of the forearm. Imaging confirms a transverse fracture at the mid-diaphysis of the right humerus. Which of the following neurovascular structures is most likely compromised due to its anatomical course along the posterior humerus?​
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Radial nerve

 

The radial nerve originates from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and travels posteriorly through the arm. 

 

It enters the posterior compartment via the triangular interval and courses along the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus, accompanied by the deep artery of the arm (profunda brachii artery). 

 

This anatomical positioning makes the radial nerve particularly susceptible to injury in midshaft humeral fractures.​

 

Clinical manifestations of radial nerve injury at this level include:

 

  • Motor deficits: Wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist extensors.
  • Sensory deficits: Numbness or paresthesia over the posterior forearm and dorsum of the hand.​

 

The deep artery of the arm, a branch of the brachial artery, accompanies the radial nerve in the radial groove, providing vascular supply to the posterior compartment of the arm.​ 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ulnar nerve: The ulnar nerve runs medially in the arm and passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. It is more commonly injured in fractures or trauma involving the medial epicondyle or elbow region, not the midshaft. 

 

Option C. Musculocutaneous nerve: This nerve innervates the anterior compartment of the arm and does not course along the humeral shaft, making it less likely to be affected by a midshaft humeral fracture.​

 

Option D. Median nerve: The median nerve travels along the medial aspect of the arm and is more susceptible to injury in supracondylar fractures or compression in the carpal tunnel, rather than midshaft humeral fractures.​

 

Educational Objective:

 

The radial nerve and the deep artery of the arm (profunda brachii) traverse the radial groove on the posterior aspect of the humerus. Midshaft fractures of the humerus can compromise these structures, leading to characteristic motor and sensory deficits.

questions.stem: The arteria thyroidea ima most commonly arises from which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Arch of aorta

 

  • The arteria thyroidea ima is an uncommon arterial variant that supplies the lower part of the thyroid gland and the trachea.
  • It most commonly originates directly from the arch of the aorta but can also arise from the brachiocephalic trunk or subclavian artery.
  • Recognition of this variant is crucial during thyroid surgeries or tracheostomies, as inadvertent injury can cause significant bleeding.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Vertebral artery: The vertebral artery ascends to supply the brainstem and posterior brain structures. It does not supply the thyroid gland.

 

Option C. External carotid artery: The external carotid artery gives rise to the superior thyroid artery, not the thyroidea ima artery.

 

Option D. Thyrocervical trunk: The thyrocervical trunk gives rise to arteries like the inferior thyroid artery, but the thyroidea ima artery typically does not arise from it.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The arteria thyroidea ima is a rare arterial branch most commonly originating from the arch of aorta and supplies the lower thyroid gland and trachea; its presence is important during surgeries involving the neck to avoid hemorrhagic complications.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is evaluated for urinary retention following pelvic surgery. Neurological examination suggests autonomic dysfunction involving the urinary bladder. Injury to which spinal nerve roots supplying the vesical plexus is most likely responsible?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) L1 & L2

 

  • The vesical plexus, supplying autonomic innervation to the urinary bladder, is derived mainly from fibers originating at the L1 and L2 spinal levels.
  • Sympathetic fibers from L1-L2 facilitate storage functions of the bladder (promoting detrusor relaxation and sphincter contraction).
  • Damage to these fibers can lead to bladder dysfunction, such as urinary retention or overflow incontinence.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. L2 & L3: These segments contribute mainly to the lumbar plexus (femoral and obturator nerves) and are not primarily involved in bladder innervation.

 

Option C. L3 & L4: L3 and L4 supply muscles of the anterior thigh and are involved in lower limb innervation, not direct autonomic control of the urinary bladder.

 

Option D. L2, L3 & L4: These levels form major parts of the lumbar plexus, but autonomic control over the bladder primarily involves L1-L2 sympathetic fibers and S2-S4 parasympathetic fibers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The sympathetic innervation of the urinary bladder via the vesical plexus arises primarily from L1 and L2 spinal segments, playing a key role in bladder storage function.

questions.stem: Which of the following arteries is primarily responsible for supplying most of the blood to the head and neck of the femur?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Medial circumflex femoral artery

 

  • The medial circumflex femoral artery is the principal artery that supplies the head and neck of the femur, especially via the posterior retinacular branches.
  • In femoral neck fractures, particularly displaced ones, there is a high risk of interruption of blood flow, leading to avascular necrosis.
  • This makes early identification and surgical management crucial in elderly patients following hip fractures.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. External pudendal artery: Supplies the skin of the lower abdomen and external genitalia, not the femoral head.

 

Option B. Lateral circumflex femoral artery: Primarily supplies the lateral thigh muscles (quadriceps) and has only a minor contribution to the femoral head.

 

Option D. Obturator artery: Gives a small acetabular branch through the ligamentum teres, but its contribution to femoral head perfusion is minimal in adults.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The medial circumflex femoral artery provides the majority of the blood supply to the femoral head and neck; disruption of this artery in femoral neck fractures predisposes to avascular necrosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male presents with instability of his knee following a sports injury. Physical examination reveals excessive anterior-posterior movement of the tibia relative to the femur. Strengthening which of the following muscles would most improve knee stability in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Quadriceps femoris

 

  • The quadriceps femoris group, consisting of rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius, plays a critical role in stabilizing the knee joint.
  • It acts by extending the knee and stabilizing the patella through the quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament.
  • Vastus medialis obliquus (VMO), a part of the vastus medialis, is especially important in preventing lateral displacement of the patella and supporting knee joint integrity.
  • Quadriceps strengthening is a key rehabilitation goal for patients with knee instability or after ligament injuries (e.g., ACL tears).

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Adductor magnus: Primarily responsible for hip adduction and minor extension of the hip, not for knee stabilization.

 

Option B. Biceps femoris: A hamstring muscle responsible for knee flexion and hip extension, but not the primary stabilizer of the knee in anterior-posterior motion.

 

Option D. Obturator internus: Functions mainly in external rotation of the hip; it has no significant role in knee stabilization.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The quadriceps femoris muscle group is essential for knee joint stability, particularly by controlling knee extension and patellar alignment, making it a critical focus in rehabilitation after knee injuries.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man presents after suffering facial trauma from a motor vehicle accident. He exhibits horizontal diplopia and cannot abduct his right eye. Imaging reveals a fracture extending into the cavernous sinus region. Which of the following cranial nerves is most likely injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Abducens nerve

 

  • The abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) passes through the cavernous sinus, running adjacent to the internal carotid artery.
  • It innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye (moves it outward).
  • Injury to the abducens nerve leads to loss of eye abduction and horizontal diplopia, particularly noticeable when the patient tries to look laterally.
  • The cavernous sinus is particularly vulnerable in cases of fractures, thrombosis, or infections spreading from facial veins.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Olfactory tract: The olfactory tract is part of the olfactory system and lies on the inferior surface of the frontal lobe, far from the cavernous sinus, and is involved in smell, not eye movements.

 

Option B. Optic nerve: The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) is related to the optic canal, not the cavernous sinus, and is involved in vision, not lateral eye movement.

 

Option D. Facial nerve: The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) travels through the internal auditory meatus and facial canal, emerging at the stylomastoid foramen — it is not located within the cavernous sinus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The abducens nerve (CN VI) runs through the cavernous sinus and controls lateral eye movement; injury to this nerve causes impaired abduction and horizontal diplopia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the normal muscle activation sequence during forearm pronation?

options.label: A
options.text: The anconeus initiates pronation, assisted later by the pronator quadratus.

options.label: B
options.text: The pronator teres initiates pronation, assisted later by the pronator quadratus.

options.label: C
options.text: The pronator quadratus initiates pronation, assisted later by the pronator teres.

options.label: D
options.text: The pronator quadratus initiates pronation, assisted later by the anconeus.

questions.answerText: The pronator quadratus initiates pronation, assisted later by the pronator teres.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The pronator quadratus initiates pronation, assisted later by the pronator teres.

 

  • Forearm pronation is primarily initiated by the pronator quadratus, a deep muscle near the distal radius and ulna.
  • Pronator quadratus starts pronation during normal activities, especially fine controlled movements.
  • Pronator teres provides additional force during rapid or resisted pronation.
  • Both muscles are innervated by the median nerve.
  • Understanding this coordinated action is crucial when assessing nerve injuries affecting forearm rotation.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The anconeus initiates pronation, assisted later by the pronator quadratus: Incorrect. The anconeus is involved in elbow extension, not forearm pronation.

 

Option B. The pronator teres initiates pronation, assisted later by the pronator quadratus: Incorrect. Pronator quadratus initiates pronation, especially for fine movements; pronator teres assists during powerful movements.

 

Option D. The pronator quadratus initiates pronation, assisted later by the anconeus: Incorrect. While pronator quadratus initiates pronation, the anconeus does not assist in pronation at all.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Forearm pronation is initiated by the pronator quadratus, particularly during fine controlled motion, and is assisted later by the pronator teres during rapid or forceful pronation.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old construction worker presents after being struck by a falling object on the side of his head. On examination, he exhibits mild swelling and tenderness behind the ear. Which of the following muscles, attached to the temporal bone, may be impacted by the trauma?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Postauricular muscle

 

The postauricular muscle is a small muscle located behind the ear, originating from the mastoid process of the temporal bone. 

 

In trauma involving swelling or injury behind the auricle, this muscle is clinically significant due to its anatomical attachment to the temporal bone. 

 

This muscle assists slightly in moving the ear and lies in the soft tissue region that would be directly affected by an impact to the side of the head. 

 

Hence, in this trauma setting, involvement of the postauricular muscle is the most appropriate consideration.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Tensor tympani muscle: The tensor tympani muscle is found inside the middle ear, where it functions to dampen sounds generated by chewing. It attaches to the malleus, not the temporal bone directly. Therefore, tensor tympani muscle is incorrect in the setting of external soft tissue injury near the auricle.

 

Option B. Stapedius muscle: The stapedius muscle is also located within the middle ear and attaches to the stapes bone, playing a key role in modulating the vibrations of the stapes in response to loud sounds. It is not externally attached to the temporal bone, making stapedius muscle the wrong choice in this clinical context.

 

Option D. Digastric muscle: The digastric muscle has two bellies. The posterior belly is attached to the mastoid notch of the temporal bone, but in cases of localized trauma behind the auricle, the postauricular muscle is more directly impacted. Therefore, digastric muscle is not the best answer here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The postauricular muscle is attached to the temporal bone and is clinically relevant in trauma or pathology affecting the soft tissues behind the auricle (ear).

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents to the emergency department with severe respiratory distress following ingestion of a small toy. On examination, the child is struggling to breathe and has an audible stridor. An emergency airway management is planned. The pediatrician explains that the narrowest part of the pediatric airway is involved in this obstruction. Which structure is most likely responsible for this narrowing?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cricoid cartilage

 

  • The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway and serves as the narrowest part of the pediatric airway.
  • In adults, the narrowest region is the glottis (vocal cords), whereas in children, it is the subglottic region at the level of the cricoid cartilage.
  • Due to this anatomical feature, airway obstructions or foreign body aspiration are more likely to cause complete airway blockage in infants and young children.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thyroid cartilage: Forms the laryngeal prominence (Adam’s apple) and does not encircle the airway.

 

Option C. Arytenoid cartilage: Helps in vocal cord movement but does not contribute to airway narrowing.

 

Option D. Epiglottis: Covers the laryngeal inlet during swallowing but is not the site of airway narrowing.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The cricoid cartilage forms a complete ring around the airway and is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway, making it a common site for obstruction and subglottic stenosis in young children.

questions.stem: A surgeon is performing a procedure in the axilla and needs to identify the divisions of the axillary artery. The axillary artery is divided into three parts based on its relation to which of the following structures?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pectoralis minor

 

  • The axillary artery is a continuation of the subclavian artery, beginning at the outer border of the first rib and extending to the lower border of the teres major muscle.
  • It is divided into three parts based on its relationship with the pectoralis minor muscle: 
    1. First part – Proximal to the pectoralis minor
    2. Second part – Posterior to the pectoralis minor
    3. Third part – Distal to the pectoralis minor

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pectoralis major: It is a superficial muscle and does not divide the axillary artery into parts.

 

Option B. Clavicle: The axillary artery begins at the outer border of the first rib, not at the clavicle.

 

Option D. Teres major: The axillary artery ends at the lower border of the teres major but is not divided by it.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The pectoralis minor muscle is the anatomical landmark that divides the axillary artery into three parts, which is important for surgical and anatomical reference.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents to the neurology clinic with complaints of difficulty walking and a history of multiple falls. On neurological examination, the knee jerk reflex is absent, while the ankle jerk reflex is preserved. Based on the reflex examination, which spinal nerve root is most likely affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) L3-L4

 

  • The knee jerk reflex (patellar reflex) is mediated by the L3-L4 nerve roots. 
  • Damage to these nerve roots leads to loss of the knee jerk reflex but preservation of other reflexes, such as the ankle jerk reflex (mediated by S1-S2).
  • Knee jerk reflex (L3-L4): Loss of this reflex indicates femoral nerve or L3-L4 radiculopathy.
  • Ankle jerk reflex (S1-S2): If present, it suggests that the sacral nerve roots are intact.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. C5-C6 (Biceps reflex): Injury to these nerve roots affects the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, not the knee jerk.

 

Option C. S1-S2 (Ankle jerk reflex): If absent, it would indicate sciatic or tibial nerve dysfunction but does not affect the knee jerk.

 

Option D. T7-T12 (Abdominal reflexes): These nerve roots control superficial abdominal reflexes, not deep tendon reflexes like the knee jerk.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The knee jerk reflex is mediated by L3-L4 and is commonly affected in lumbar radiculopathy or femoral nerve dysfunction. 
  • Preservation of the ankle jerk reflex (S1-S2) helps localize the lesion to the upper lumbar region.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old construction worker presents with difficulty raising his shoulder and shrugging after sustaining a neck injury at work. Examination reveals weakness in shoulder elevation and lateral scapular winging. Injury to which of the following nerves is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Accessory nerve

 

  • The trapezius muscle, responsible for elevating the shoulder and scapular retraction, is innervated by the accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI). 
  • Damage to this nerve leads to:
  • Weakness in shrugging the shoulder
  • Lateral scapular winging, as the trapezius helps stabilize the scapula
  • This condition is commonly seen after neck trauma or radical neck surgery.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thoracodorsal nerve: Innervates latissimus dorsi, responsible for adduction, extension, and medial rotation of the arm.

 

Option B. Dorsal scapular nerve: Innervates levator scapulae and rhomboids, involved in scapular elevation and retraction.

 

Option D. Suprascapular nerve: Innervates supraspinatus and infraspinatus, affecting arm abduction and external rotation, but not scapular movement.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. 
  • Injury to this nerve leads to scapular winging and weakness in shoulder shrugging, commonly seen after neck trauma or surgery.

questions.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman presents for her first prenatal visit at 12 weeks of gestation. She admits to poor dietary habits and lack of prenatal vitamin supplementation. A fetal ultrasound reveals a defect as shown below. This condition results from failure of closure of which of the following structures?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Posterior neuropore

 

  • Neural tube defects (NTDs) occur due to failure of proper neural tube closure during early embryonic development (by the 4th week of gestation). 
  • The posterior neuropore gives rise to the spinal cord and its coverings. Failure of its closure leads to spina bifida, meningocele, meningomyelocele, and myeloschisis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior neuropore: Its failure results in anencephaly or encephalocele.

 

Option C. Neural crest cells: These give rise to peripheral nervous system structures and do not contribute to neural tube closure.

 

Option D. Somites: These contribute to vertebral formation and musculature but do not directly cause neural tube closure defects.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Failure of posterior neuropore closure leads to spina bifida and related defects. Folic acid supplementation before and during pregnancy significantly reduces the risk.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the medial branch of the external carotid artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ascending pharyngeal artery

 

  • The ascending pharyngeal artery (APA) is the only medial branch of the external carotid artery. 
  • It is the smallest branch and arises close to the origin of the external carotid artery. 
  • The APA supplies several structures, including the pharynx, prevertebral muscles, middle ear, and cranial meninges.

 

Branches of the External Carotid Artery:

 

  • Anterior branches: Superior thyroid, lingual, and facial arteries.
  • Posterior branches: Occipital and posterior auricular arteries.
  • Medial branch: Ascending pharyngeal artery (the only medial branch).
  • Terminal branches: Superficial temporal and maxillary arteries.

 

Clinical Relevance:

 

  • The ascending pharyngeal artery plays an essential role in vascularizing the pharynx and may be involved in cases of epistaxis or tumors in the nasopharyngeal region.
  • Due to its small size and deep location, it is often overlooked in superficial dissections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lingual artery: Incorrect. This is an anterior branch of the external carotid artery and supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth.

 

Option B. Facial artery: Incorrect. This is another anterior branch, supplying the face and oral cavity.

 

Option D. Posterior auricular artery: Incorrect. This is a posterior branch of the external carotid artery, supplying the auricle and scalp behind the ear.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The ascending pharyngeal artery is the only medial branch of the external carotid artery and the smallest branch, supplying the pharynx, middle ear, and meninges.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with diplopia and vertical gaze disturbance. On examination, she is unable to look downward when the eye is adducted. An MRI reveals a small lesion affecting a cranial nerve within the anterior aspect of the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. Which structure is most likely involved?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Trochlear nucleus

 

  • The trochlear nucleus is located in the anterior midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. 
  • It gives rise to fibers that decussate and exit dorsally. 
  • Lesions here result in dysfunction of the superior oblique muscle, which impairs downward gaze, especially in the adducted position (like reading or walking downstairs).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Oculomotor nerve: Lesion causes ptosis, "down and out" eye, and pupil dilation—not isolated downward gaze paralysis.

 

Option C. Medial longitudinal fasciculus: Causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus).

 

Option D. Abducens nucleus: Causes horizontal gaze palsy due to impaired lateral rectus control, not vertical gaze problems.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Lesions affecting the trochlear nucleus in the midbrain impair superior oblique function, resulting in vertical diplopia that worsens with downward gaze in adduction.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and a sensation of food getting stuck in his throat. He also complains of chronic halitosis. A barium swallow study reveals a posterior outpouching in the hypopharynx. Which of the following anatomical structures is most likely involved in the formation of this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Killian's dehiscence

 

  • Killian's dehiscence is a weak area in the posterior pharyngeal wall located between the oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus and the transverse fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscles of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. 
  • This area is prone to herniation, leading to Zenker’s diverticulum, a pharyngeal pouch that presents with dysphagia, regurgitation, halitosis, and chronic aspiration. A barium swallow is the diagnostic test of choice.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Killian-Jamieson area: This area is anterolateral to the cricopharyngeus muscle and is another site of potential herniation, though much less common. Herniations here lead to Killian-Jamieson diverticulum, which is anterior and does not present as Zenker’s diverticulum does.

 

Option C. Laimer’s triangle: This is an area of weakness below the cricopharyngeus muscle and is associated with esophageal diverticula rather than pharyngeal diverticula.

 

Option D. Zenker’s triangle: This term is not commonly used in clinical practice; Zenker’s diverticulum actually originates from Killian’s dehiscence.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Killian's dehiscence is a weak anatomical area between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles, predisposing individuals to Zenker’s diverticulum. 
  • This condition presents with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, and aspiration pneumonia. 
  • Diagnosis is made via barium swallow, and definitive treatment involves cricopharyngeal myotomy with or without diverticulectomy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old professional singer presents with hoarseness of voice that worsens after prolonged use. Laryngoscopic examination reveals dysfunction of the muscle responsible for increasing the pitch of the voice. Which of the following muscles is most likely affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Cricothyroid

 

  • The cricothyroid muscle is responsible for tensing and lengthening the vocal folds, which increases the pitch of the voice. 
  • Dysfunction of this muscle, often due to damage to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, results in inability to modulate pitch, leading to hoarseness and difficulty in producing high-pitched sounds. 
  • This is particularly important in singers or voice professionals.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thyroarytenoid: Shortens and relaxes the vocal cords, decreasing pitch. It is not responsible for increasing pitch.

 

Option B. Posterior cricoarytenoid: The only muscle that abducts the vocal folds, opening the glottis. It plays a role in respiration but not in pitch modulation.

 

Option D. Lateral cricoarytenoid: Adducts the vocal folds, bringing them together. It is involved in phonation but does not affect pitch control.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The cricothyroid muscle is the primary pitch-modulating muscle of the larynx, tensing the vocal folds to increase pitch. 
  • It is innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and damage to this nerve (e.g., during thyroid surgery) results in difficulty with high-pitched sounds.

questions.stemHtml: A newborn presents with weakness in the hand and forearm following a difficult breech delivery. Examination reveals deformity as shown below. There is also associated Horner's syndrome with ptosis and miosis. Which part of the brachial plexus is most likely injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Lower trunk (C8-T1)

 

  • The clinical features in this neonate are characteristic of Klumpke’s palsy, a brachial plexus injury affecting the lower trunk (C8-T1). This occurs due to excessive arm abduction, such as in breech delivery with arm hyperextension or a fall where one grabs an object to prevent falling.

 

Key features:

 

  • Paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals, interossei, thenar, hypothenar muscles)
  • "Claw hand" deformity – Hyperextension at MCP joints, flexion at IP joints
  • Weakness in wrist and finger flexors
  • Associated Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) – Due to damage to sympathetic fibers traveling with T1

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Upper trunk: (C5-C6) Injury results in Erb-Duchenne palsy seen in shoulder dystocia during delivery. Features include "waiter's tip" deformity (adducted, internally rotated arm with extended elbow).

 

Option B. Middle trunk: (C7) Rarely injured in isolation, may contribute to weakness in elbow extension and wrist flexion.

 

Option D. Posterior cord: Injury affects radial nerve, leading to wrist drop due to paralysis of extensor muscles of the forearm.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Klumpke’s palsy (C8-T1 injury) occurs due to excessive arm abduction and presents with claw hand deformity and possible Horner’s syndrome due to T1 involvement.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female presents with numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger, especially at night. She works as a secretary and spends long hours typing. Examination reveals positive Tinel's and Phalen's tests. If left untreated, which of the following complications is most likely to occur?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thenar muscle atrophy

 

  • Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) occurs due to compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel. 
  • The median nerve innervates the thenar muscles, and chronic compression can lead to thenar muscle atrophy, resulting in weakness of thumb opposition, abduction, and fine motor function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hypothenar muscle atrophy: The ulnar nerve innervates the hypothenar muscles, not the median nerve. Ulnar nerve compression occurs in Guyon’s canal syndrome, not in CTS.

 

Option C. Wrist drop: This is a sign of radial nerve injury, which affects the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers, not the median nerve.

 

Option D. Loss of wrist flexion: Although the median nerve partially contributes to wrist flexion, significant weakness of wrist flexion occurs in proximal median nerve injuries, not in CTS.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) results from median nerve compression in the wrist, leading to paresthesia in the lateral 3½ fingers. 
  • Chronic cases can result in thenar muscle atrophy and impaired thumb function, making early diagnosis and treatment essential.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male boxer presents with wrist pain after falling onto an outstretched hand during training. Examination reveals tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. The physician is concerned about a fracture of the underlying bone. Which of the following bones is most likely injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Scaphoid

 

  • The anatomical snuffbox is a triangular depression located on the lateral wrist. Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal bone fractures and occur due to falls onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH injury).
    • Classic finding: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox
    • Complication: Risk of avascular necrosis due to retrograde blood supply from the radial artery

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lunate: More commonly associated with perilunate dislocations rather than fractures.

 

Option B. Capitate: Less commonly fractured; usually involved in high-energy trauma.

 

Option D. Hamate: Typically fractured due to direct trauma (e.g., from a baseball bat or golf club).

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Scaphoid fractures should always be suspected in patients with wrist trauma and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. 
  • Due to its retrograde blood supply, scaphoid fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis, necessitating early diagnosis and immobilization.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with dizziness, ataxia, dysmetria, and nystagmus. He reports difficulty coordinating his movements and maintaining balance. On examination, he has an intention tremor, hypotonia, and gait disturbances. Which of the following arteries is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Superior cerebellar artery (SCA)

 

  • The superior cerebellar artery (SCA) arises from the basilar artery and supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum, the roof nuclei, and parts of the midbrain.
  • Thrombosis or infarction of the SCA leads to: 
    • Ataxia (loss of coordination)
    • Dysmetria (impaired ability to control distance of movements)
    • Nystagmus (involuntary eye movements)
    • Intention tremors
    • Vertigo and dizziness

 

Other Options:


Option A. Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA):

 

  • Supplies the anterior and inferior cerebellum, pons, and inner ear.
  • Infarction causes AICA syndrome, which includes vertigo, hearing loss, and facial paralysis.


Option B. Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA):

 

  • Supplies the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum.
  • Occlusion causes Wallenberg syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome), presenting with dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral facial numbness, and contralateral body pain/temp loss.


Option D. Vertebral Artery:

 

  • Affects multiple brainstem and cerebellar regions, leading to brainstem syndromes with bilateral symptoms.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The superior cerebellar artery (SCA) supplies the superior cerebellum and midbrain structures. 
  • SCA infarcts present with ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremors, and vertigo due to cerebellar dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease and hypertension presents with sudden onset of chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis. He is found to have an acute myocardial infarction affecting the posterior wall of the left ventricle. Angiography reveals that the artery supplying the posterior interventricular septum and posterior wall of the heart is occluded. Given this information, which of the following arteries is most likely responsible for the blood supply to this region?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Posterior descending artery (PDA)

 

  • The posterior descending artery (PDA) is the primary vessel responsible for supplying the posterior third of the interventricular septum and parts of the posterior wall of the left ventricle.
  • The PDA typically arises from the right coronary artery (RCA) in about 85% of individuals with right-dominant circulation.
  • In these individuals, occlusion of the RCA will affect the PDA, leading to ischemia in the posterior wall of the left ventricle and posterior septum, resulting in a posterior myocardial infarction.
  • In the remaining 15% of individuals with left-dominant circulation, the PDA arises from the left circumflex artery (LCX).
  • However, since the question specifies that the artery supplying the posterior wall and septum is occluded, it points to the PDA as the direct vessel involved.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Left anterior descending artery (LAD): The LAD supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, and part of the apex of the heart. Occlusion of the LAD would result in an anterior or anteroseptal myocardial infarction, not a posterior infarction.

 

Option B. Left circumflex artery (LCX): The LCX primarily supplies the lateral and posterior aspects of the left ventricle in left-dominant circulation. However, unless the PDA arises from the LCX in left-dominant circulation, the LCX alone does not directly supply the posterior interventricular septum and posterior left ventricle. Since the PDA is mentioned as supplying the posterior septum and wall, LCX is not the best choice in this case.

 

Option C. Right coronary artery (RCA): While the RCA often gives rise to the PDA in right-dominant circulation, it is not the RCA itself that directly supplies the posterior wall of the left ventricle. The PDA, which arises from the RCA in right-dominant circulation, is the more precise answer to the question.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The posterior descending artery (PDA) is responsible for supplying the posterior interventricular septum and the posterior wall of the left ventricle.
  • In the majority of individuals with right-dominant circulation, the PDA arises from the right coronary artery (RCA).
  • Occlusion of the PDA leads to ischemia in the posterior aspects of the heart.

questions.stemHtml: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents due to concerns about delayed eruption of his permanent teeth and abnormal appearance of his shoulders. Physical examination reveals a wide, flat skull, midface hypoplasia, and the ability to bring his shoulders together in front of his chest. X-rays of the chest are shown below. Which of the following skeletal abnormalities is most characteristic of this condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Craniosynostosis with premature fusion of sutures

options.label: D
options.text: Multiple exostoses (bony outgrowths) on long bones

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Hypoplasia or absence of clavicles

 

  • The X-ray image of the chest in this case shows underdeveloped or absent clavicles, which is a hallmark feature of cleidocranial dysostosis (also known as cleidocranial dysplasia).
  • In a normal chest X-ray, the clavicles (collarbones) are clearly visible as long, horizontal bones at the top of the rib cage, just beneath the shoulders.
  • However, in this patient, the clavicles appear hypoplastic (underdeveloped) or absent, allowing the patient to approximate their shoulders in front of the chest—a characteristic finding in this condition.
  • This feature allows affected individuals to approximate their shoulders in front of their chest, which is a classic finding.
  • The condition also presents with other skeletal anomalies, including a wide, flat skull (brachycephaly), midface hypoplasia, and delayed eruption of permanent teeth.
  • The skeletal abnormalities stem from mutations in the RUNX2 gene, which is critical for osteoblast differentiation and proper bone formation, particularly impacting the development of the clavicles and craniofacial bones.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Craniosynostosis with premature fusion of sutures: Incorrect. Craniosynostosis involves the premature fusion of skull sutures, leading to restricted skull growth and an abnormal head shape. In contrast, cleidocranial dysostosis is characterized by delayed closure of fontanelles, resulting in a broad, flat skull, not early suture closure.

 

Option C. Absence of radius and thumb: Incorrect. The absence of the radius and thumb is typically seen in radial ray anomalies, which are features of conditions like Holt-Oram syndrome or Fanconi anemia. These are not characteristic findings in cleidocranial dysostosis, which primarily affects the clavicles and skull bones.

 

Option D. Multiple exostoses (bony outgrowths) on long bones: Incorrect. Multiple exostoses are a hallmark of hereditary multiple exostoses (osteochondromatosis), where patients develop benign bony outgrowths. This is not seen in cleidocranial dysostosis, where skeletal involvement is more focused on the clavicles and craniofacial bones.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Cleidocranial dysostosis is characterized by hypoplasia or absence of clavicles, which allows for excessive shoulder mobility, delayed closure of the fontanelles, and dental abnormalities such as delayed tooth eruption.
  • It is caused by mutations in the RUNX2 gene, which is essential for normal bone formation and osteoblast differentiation.
  • Recognizing these skeletal features is critical for diagnosing the condition.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of right-sided facial paralysis, inability to close her right eye, and loss of taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of her tongue. Physical examination reveals drooping of the right side of her face and absence of the corneal reflex on the right. Imaging reveals a lesion at the base of the skull affecting the cranial nerve as it exits through its respective foramen. Which foramen is most likely involved in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Internal acoustic meatus

 

  • This patient's presentation of sudden right-sided facial paralysis, inability to close the eye, and loss of taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is consistent with a lesion of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).
  • The facial nerve is responsible for motor control of the muscles of facial expression, taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and innervation to the lacrimal and salivary glands.
  • It also contributes to the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.
  • The facial nerve (CN VII) exits the skull through the internal acoustic meatus, along with the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).
  • A lesion at this location, such as from a tumor or other compressive pathology, can result in facial paralysis and loss of taste sensation as seen in this patient.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Foramen ovale: The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V3). This nerve is responsible for sensory innervation to the lower face and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication. A lesion affecting the foramen ovale would present with loss of sensation in the mandibular distribution and difficulty with mastication, not facial paralysis or loss of taste sensation.

 

Option C. Jugular foramen: The jugular foramen transmits cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), and XI (accessory). A lesion here would cause deficits such as dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), hoarseness (vocal cord paralysis), and shoulder weakness (due to accessory nerve involvement), but not facial paralysis or loss of taste on the anterior tongue.

 

Option D. Hypoglossal canal: The hypoglossal canal transmits the hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII), which controls the muscles of the tongue. Lesions here cause weakness or atrophy of the tongue muscles, typically with deviation of the tongue to the side of the lesion when protruded, but this would not cause facial paralysis or taste disturbances.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) exits the skull via the internal acoustic meatus and is responsible for motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression, taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and innervation to the lacrimal and salivary glands.
  • A lesion affecting the internal acoustic meatus can result in facial paralysis and loss of taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with lower back pain that worsens with bending and twisting movements. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the lower lumbar region, particularly around the lateral abdominal wall, suggesting involvement of a muscle that stabilizes the lumbar spine and aids in lateral flexion of the trunk. Which of the following nerves most likely innervates the affected muscle?

options.label: A
options.text: Subcostal nerve (T12) and anterior branches of L1-L4

questions.answerText: Subcostal nerve (T12) and anterior branches of L1-L4
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Subcostal nerve (T12) and anterior branches of L1-L4

 

  • The quadratus lumborum muscle is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12) and the anterior branches of the lumbar nerves L1-L4.
  • This muscle is located in the posterior abdominal wall and extends from the 12th rib to the iliac crest, attaching to the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae.
  • Its functions include stabilizing the lumbar spine, assisting in lateral flexion of the trunk, and fixing the 12th rib during forced expiration.
  • Injury or strain to the quadratus lumborum can result in lower back pain, particularly with movements that involve bending or twisting, as these actions engage this muscle.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Femoral nerve: Incorrect. The femoral nerve originates from L2-L4 and innervates muscles of the anterior thigh, such as the quadriceps femoris and iliopsoas. It is not involved in innervating the quadratus lumborum, which is located in the posterior abdominal wall.

 

Option C. Obturator nerve: Incorrect. The obturator nerve arises from L2-L4 and supplies the medial compartment of the thigh, innervating muscles like the adductors. It does not contribute to the innervation of the quadratus lumborum.

 

Option D. Ilioinguinal nerve: Incorrect. The ilioinguinal nerve arises from L1 and provides sensory innervation to the inguinal region and lower abdominal wall. Although it is in proximity to the quadratus lumborum, it does not innervate this muscle directly.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The quadratus lumborum muscle is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12) and the anterior branches of L1-L4 from the lumbar plexus.
  • It plays a key role in stabilizing the lumbar spine, lateral flexion of the trunk, and fixing the 12th rib during respiration.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old athlete sustains an injury to his Achilles tendon and requires surgical repair using a tendon graft. The surgeon selects a tendon that is commonly harvested for grafting procedures in the lower limb due to its small size and minimal impact on function. Which of the following tendons is most likely used for grafting in this scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Plantaris

 

  • The plantaris tendon is often used in tendon grafting procedures, particularly for lower limb reconstructions like Achilles tendon repairs.
  • The plantaris is a small, thin muscle with a long tendon that runs alongside the Achilles tendon. It is easily harvested and can be used as a graft due to its length and strength.
  • Its removal typically has minimal impact on the function of the lower limb because the plantaris muscle is considered vestigial and contributes little to overall movement.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Gracilis: Incorrect. The gracilis tendon, located in the medial thigh, is sometimes used as a graft, particularly in conjunction with the semitendinosus tendon for procedures like ACL reconstruction. However, it is not the preferred choice for smaller grafting needs, such as those involving the Achilles tendon, where the plantaris tendon is more suitable.

 

Option C. Tibialis posterior: Incorrect. The tibialis posterior is a major muscle of the lower leg that plays a critical role in supporting the arch of the foot and in plantarflexion. Its tendon is not typically harvested for grafting due to its essential role in foot stability and movement.

 

Option D. Palmaris longus: Incorrect. The palmaris longus is a tendon located in the forearm and is often used for grafting in upper limb procedures, such as hand and wrist reconstructions. It is not typically used in lower limb grafting procedures like those involving the Achilles tendon.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The plantaris tendon is commonly used for tendon grafting in lower limb surgical procedures, such as Achilles tendon repair, due to its accessibility and minimal impact on function.
  • Its role as a vestigial muscle makes it a good choice for small grafting needs without compromising lower limb movement.
