questions.stemHtml: A 11-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after falling from a height. He complains of severe pain on the right side of his chest. Examination reveals tenderness at the midaxillary line, and imaging shows a rib fracture with accumulation of blood in the pleural space, causing a hemothorax and atelectasis. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Intercostal vessels

 

  • The intercostal vessels run along the inferior margin of each rib in the intercostal spaces, making them vulnerable to injury when there is a rib fracture.
  • In this case, the rib fracture at the midaxillary line likely caused damage to the intercostal arteries and veins, leading to bleeding into the pleural space and subsequent hemothorax.
  • The intercostal arteries branch off the thoracic aorta, while the intercostal veins drain into the azygos system.
  • Injury to these vessels can cause significant bleeding, particularly in the context of trauma such as a fall, leading to complications like hemothorax and atelectasis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Left common carotid artery: Incorrect. The left common carotid artery supplies the head and neck, originating from the aortic arch. It is not located near the ribs or pleural space and would not be affected by a rib fracture. Injury to this vessel would lead to neck or upper chest bleeding, not a hemothorax from rib trauma.

 

Option C. Subclavian artery: Incorrect. The subclavian artery is located above the first rib and beneath the clavicle. It supplies blood to the upper limbs and parts of the chest. While it can be injured in severe trauma, it is not directly related to rib fractures at the midaxillary line. Damage to the subclavian artery would cause bleeding in the upper chest or shoulder region rather than a hemothorax from a rib injury.

 

Option D. Thoracic duct: Incorrect. The thoracic duct is the main lymphatic channel in the body, draining lymph into the left subclavian vein. Injury to the thoracic duct can result in a chylothorax (accumulation of lymph in the pleural space), but it would not cause a hemothorax. It is also less likely to be injured from a rib fracture compared to the intercostal vessels.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Intercostal vessels are a common source of bleeding in cases of rib fractures, as they run along the inferior margin of each rib and can be damaged by fractures.
  • Injury to these vessels can lead to a hemothorax, which is the accumulation of blood in the pleural space, potentially causing atelectasis and difficulty breathing.

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man presents with chronic joint pain and reduced mobility in his knee. Imaging reveals degenerative changes in the knee joint, prompting a biopsy of the joint cartilage. The histopathological image of the cartilage is shown below. Based on the microscopic appearance, which of the following types of cartilage is most likely present?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) White fibrocartilage

 

  • The image shows prominent collagen fibers arranged in bundles with intervening rows of chondrocytes, characteristic of white fibrocartilage.
  • Fibrocartilage is found in structures that require tensile strength and shock absorption, such as the intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, and menisci of the knee.
  • The dense collagenous matrix helps resist compression and shear forces, making it ideal for supporting weight and maintaining joint integrity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Articular hyaline cartilage: Incorrect. Hyaline cartilage is characterized by a smooth, glassy matrix with scattered chondrocytes in lacunae and minimal visible collagen fibers. It forms the articular surfaces of most joints, providing a smooth surface for joint movement. The image does not show the typical homogeneous appearance of hyaline cartilage.

 

Option B. Non-articular hyaline cartilage: Incorrect. Non-articular hyaline cartilage is similar in appearance to articular hyaline cartilage but is found in locations like the trachea and nasal septum. The given image shows collagen fiber bundles, which are not characteristic of hyaline cartilage.

 

Option D. Yellow cartilage: Incorrect. Yellow cartilage, also known as elastic cartilage, contains elastic fibers in addition to collagen. It is found in the external ear, epiglottis, and eustachian tube. The image does not show the characteristic elastin network seen in yellow cartilage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • White fibrocartilage is characterized by dense collagen bundles and is found in structures that require high tensile strength, such as the menisci and intervertebral discs.

questions.stem: Which of the following muscles is most likely not innervated by the superior gluteal nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Piriformis

 

  • The superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) innervates the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae muscles, which are involved in hip abduction and stabilizing the pelvis during walking.
  • The piriformis muscle, however, is innervated by the nerve to the piriformis (branches of S1 and S2).
  • Therefore, any muscle dysfunction not related to these three muscles suggests the involvement of a muscle like the piriformis, which has a different innervation.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Tensor fasciae latae: Incorrect. This muscle is innervated by the superior gluteal nerve and contributes to hip abduction and internal rotation. It is not the muscle excluded from innervation by this nerve.

 

Option B. Gluteus minimus: Incorrect. The gluteus minimus is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve and assists in hip abduction and internal rotation. It is innervated by the superior gluteal nerve, making it an incorrect choice.

 

Option D. Gluteus medius: Incorrect. The gluteus medius is also innervated by the superior gluteal nerve and plays a key role in stabilizing the pelvis during walking and hip abduction. This makes it the wrong choice as well.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The superior gluteal nerve provides innervation to the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae, but not the piriformis, which is supplied by the nerve to the piriformis.



ore, any muscle dysfunction not related to these three muscles suggests the involvement of a muscle like the piriformis, which has a different innervation.

questions.stemHtml: A 51-year-old man presents with visual disturbances affecting the central field of vision. An MRI of the brain is performed, revealing the involvement of a specific sulcus in the occipital lobe, as indicated by the arrow in the provided image. Which of the following sulci is identified in the given coronal section?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Calcarine sulcus

 

  • The calcarine sulcus is a prominent sulcus located in the occipital lobe, extending from the parieto-occipital sulcus to the posterior pole of the brain.
  • It plays a crucial role in the primary visual cortex (V1), which is responsible for processing visual information, including central vision.
  • In this MRI, the arrow points to a location consistent with the calcarine sulcus, making this the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Marginal sulcus: The marginal sulcus is part of the cingulate sulcus that extends to the medial aspect of the brain. It is not involved in the visual processing of central vision and is located more anteriorly compared to the calcarine sulcus.

 

Option C. Parieto-occipital sulcus: This sulcus separates the parietal and occipital lobes but is not directly involved in the processing of visual information in the primary visual cortex. It is located more anteriorly relative to the calcarine sulcus.

 

Option D. Lingual sulcus: The lingual sulcus is related to the lingual gyrus, which is also involved in visual processing but is not the primary visual cortex like the calcarine sulcus. The sulcus identified in the image is more consistent with the location of the calcarine sulcus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The calcarine sulcus is located in the occipital lobe and is integral to the function of the primary visual cortex.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy tripped while running in a playground, sustained lacerations at the base of his thumb from a broken glass bottle. Examination revealed that he could not oppose his thumb to his fingers, and there was weakness in thumb abduction and flexion. No sensory deficits were noted. Which nerve was most likely injured?

options.label: A
options.text: Superficial palmar branch of median nerve

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Recurrent branch of median nerve

 

  • This branch of the median nerve is specifically responsible for motor control of the thenar muscles, which facilitate thumb opposition, abduction, and flexion.
  • The clinical symptoms of inability to oppose the thumb, coupled with weakness in abduction and flexion, directly correlate with an injury to this nerve.
  • The absence of sensory deficits aligns with the recurrent branch's predominantly motor function.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Superficial palmar branch of median nerve: This nerve primarily provides sensory innervation to the palm of the hand and does not influence motor functions, making it less likely to be involved given the motor deficits described.

 

Option C. Deep branch of ulnar nerve: This nerve affects the ulnar side of the hand, influencing the intrinsic muscles but not primarily responsible for thumb movements, which are crucially controlled by the median nerve.

 

Option D. Radial nerve: Typically, responsible for wrist and finger extension. While it also innervates some muscles involved in thumb abduction (such as the extensor pollicis longus and brevis), its primary functions do not include opposition or the specific type of flexion described.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The recurrent branch of the median nerve is critical for thumb movements including opposition, abduction, and flexion.
  • Injury to this nerve results in characteristic deficits of these thumb functions without affecting sensation, highlighting its importance in thumb motor control.

questions.stem: Which structure should be incised to safely access the omental bursa while protecting the structures entering the porta hepatitis and the blood vessels supplying the stomach?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hepatoduodenal portion of lesser omentum

 

  • This is the optimal choice for incision when needing access to the omental bursa during abdominal surgeries.
  • It strategically avoids the portal triad and other vital structures, providing a direct route to the omental bursa without compromising the vascular or structural integrity of the liver or stomach.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Superior layer of coronary ligament: This ligament secures the liver to the diaphragm and does not provide direct or safe access to the omental bursa.

 

Option C. Gastrohepatic ligament: Part of the lesser omentum, but less ideal than the hepatoduodenal portion because it has significant vascular structures that may be at risk during incision.

 

Option D. Gastrosplenic ligament: This ligament connects the stomach to the spleen and is not relevant for accessing the omental bursa; incising it could risk injury to the stomach and spleen vasculature.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Selecting the hepatoduodenal portion of the lesser omentum for incision during surgical approaches to the omental bursa is critical for avoiding damage to key vascular and structural components in the upper abdomen.
  • This choice is crucial for successful surgical outcomes and patient safety during complex abdominal procedures.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old male underwent ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) reconstruction surgery in the lithotomy position, with support at the popliteal fossae and proximal tibiae but not at the ankles. The day after surgery, he reported reduced sensation on the lateral side of his right leg and foot and had difficulty dorsiflexing his right foot. Given the postoperative symptoms of decreased lateral leg and foot sensation and dorsiflexion difficulty, which muscle innervated by the implicated nerve is likely affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Extensor Digitorum Longus

 

  • This muscle is innervated by the peroneal nerve, which is susceptible to compression when the knee's lateral area is unsupported in surgery.
  • The peroneal nerve's impairment would lead to the reported symptoms, specifically affecting dorsiflexion and lateral foot sensation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Flexor Hallucis Longus: Innervated by the tibial nerve, not typically associated with the described symptoms.

 

Option B. Abductor Hallucis: Also innervated by the tibial nerve and medial plantar nerve unrelated to dorsiflexion or lateral sensory changes.

 

Option D. Semi-Membranosus: Innervated by tibial portion of the sciatic nerve; involvement would not result in the specific symptoms described.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The peroneal nerve, vulnerable to pressure near the fibular head during certain surgical positions, is crucial for foot dorsiflexion and lateral leg sensation.
  • Its damage can lead to significant functional impairments, underscoring the importance of proper limb positioning during surgery to prevent such issues.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man experiences palpitations and dizziness. An echocardiogram shows an enlarged right atrium with a right-to-left shunt. During cardiac catheterization, a valve-like structure is observed near the coronary sinus. Which structure, noted during cardiac catheterization guarding the coronary sinus, could be associated with the patient's symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thebesian Valve

 

  • This valve guards the opening of the coronary sinus in the right atrium and can vary in size and competency among individuals.
  • It is significant in this scenario because its presence and potential dysfunction or abnormality could influence the flow dynamics of the heart, particularly noted during the observed right-to-left shunt in the echocardiogram.
  • The valve’s role in potentially contributing to unusual cardiac shunts or obstructing coronary sinus flow
  • could relate directly to the patient's symptoms of palpitations and dizziness.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Eustachian Valve: Located at the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium, this valve is more involved in fetal circulation and typically less influential in postnatal right-to-left shunts directly affecting the coronary sinus.

 

Option C. Crista Terminalis: A muscular ridge that separates the smooth and trabeculated parts of the right atrium, not a valve and not directly involved in guarding any openings.

 

Option D. Mitral Valve: Located between the left atrium and left ventricle, completely unrelated to the right atrium or coronary sinus anatomy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The Thebesian Valve, guarding the coronary sinus, plays a critical role in venous return from the myocardium to the right atrium and could influence cardiac symptoms if abnormal or dysfunctional, as observed in conditions presenting with cardiac shunt symptoms.

questions.stem: In a histology lecture, students learn about unique histopathological features of different organs. The professor discusses corpora amylacea, asking the students to identify the organ where these structures are typically found. Where are corpora amylacea most commonly found?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Prostate

 

  • Corpora amylacea are commonly found in the prostate gland, especially as men age.
  • These structures are benign, laminated, concentric, calcific deposits that can be seen during microscopic examination of prostatic tissue.
  • They are thought to result from the secretions of prostate cells and do not usually have clinical significance unless they are abundant and associated with inflammatory conditions.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pineal gland: While the pineal gland does contain calcifications known as "brain sand" or pineal sand, these are not referred to as corpora amylacea.

 

Option B. Penis: Corpora amylacea are not associated with penile tissue.

 

Option C. Bladder: Although the bladder can develop calcifications and other deposits, especially in conditions like chronic inflammation, these are not termed corpora amylacea.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Corpora amylacea are characteristic microscopic features commonly found in the prostate gland, particularly in elderly individuals.
  • Their presence is typically benign and represents accumulated prostatic secretions that have undergone calcification.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man, hard of hearing, while riding his motorbike met with a head-on collision with the truck on a national highway. He was thrown off the motorbike and fell down with an impact on his back a few metres away from the accident site. He was received in casualty. X-ray pictures taken showed multiple fractures of the left scapula. Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Suprascapular artery passes above the suprascapular notch

options.label: B
options.text: Suprascapular nerve arises at Erb's point

options.label: C
options.text: If suprascapular nerve is injured at spinoglenoid notch medial rotation of arm is affected

options.label: D
options.text: Articular branches to acromioclavicular joint arises from suprascapular nerve proximal to suprascapular notch

questions.answerText: If suprascapular nerve is injured at spinoglenoid notch medial rotation of arm is affected
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) If Suprascapular Nerve is injured at Spinoglenoid Notch medial rotation of arm is affected

 

  • The suprascapular nerve primarily innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. These muscles are involved in the abduction and lateral rotation of the shoulder, respectively.
  • If the suprascapular nerve is injured at the spinoglenoid notch, it would predominantly affect the infraspinatus muscle, leading to difficulties in lateral rotation of the arm, not medial rotation.
  • This statement is incorrect. Injury to the suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch would impact lateral rotation, not medial rotation.
  • Suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus (initiates abduction upto 90 degree), then passes through spinoglenoid notch to supply infraspinatus (lateral rotator of arm).
  • Types of Scapular Fracture:

 

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Suprascapular artery passes above the suprascapular notch:

 

  • The suprascapular artery typically passes over the suprascapular notch, while the suprascapular nerve passes under it through this notch.
  • Mnemonic:
    • N for Nerve , N for Navy (Navy is under water)
    • A for Artery , A for Air (Air is above)

 

 

 

Option B. Suprascapular nerve arises at Erb's point:

 

  • The Suprascapular Nerve originates from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, which is formed by the union of the C5 and C6 nerve roots.
  • Erb's point refers to a site near the neck where nerves from the brachial plexus converge and are superficial enough to be impacted by trauma.

 

 

 

Option D. Articular branches to acromioclavicular joint arises from suprascapular nerve proximal to suprascapular notch:

 

  • The suprascapular nerve does give off articular branches to the shoulder joint, including the acromioclavicular joint. These branches typically arise before the nerve passes through the suprascapular notch.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • If Suprascapular Nerve is Injured at Spinoglenoid Notch Medial Rotation of Arm is Affected:

  • If the suprascapular nerve is injured at the spinoglenoid notch, it would predominantly affect the infraspinatus muscle, leading to difficulties in lateral rotation of the arm, not medial rotation.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset weakness and loss of sensation on the right side of his body. Neurological examination reveals contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss affecting the face, arm, and leg. Which of the following is the most common cause of stroke involving the Internal Capsule?

options.label: B
options.text: Direct branches of internal carotid artery

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral striate branches of middle cerebral artery

questions.answerText: Lateral striate branches of middle cerebral artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Lateral striate branches of middle cerebral artery

 

  • Stroke of internal capsule is most commonly caused by occlusion of lateral striate branches of middle cerebral artery also called Charcot’s artery of cerebral hemorrhage.
  •  It supplies posterior limb of internal capsule
  • Lateral Striate Branches of Middle Cerebral Artery are small, deep penetrating arteries, also known as lenticulostriate arteries, which branch from the MCA.
  • They supply blood to parts of the basal ganglia and the internal capsule.  The lateral striate arteries are the primary suppliers of blood to the internal capsule.
  • Due to their small size and critical location, these arteries are particularly susceptible to hypertension-induced damage, leading to lacunar strokes, which often occur in the internal capsule.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior cerebral artery: Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) primarily supplies the medial surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the anterior four-fifths of the corpus callosum. Although important for the blood supply to the frontal lobes and superior medial parietal lobes, the ACA is not typically involved in supplying the internal capsule.

 

Option B. Direct branches of internal carotid artery: The internal carotid artery branches into several major arteries, including the middle cerebral artery and the anterior cerebral artery. While the internal carotid artery is a major supplier of blood to the brain, it does not directly supply the internal capsule.

 

Option D. Recurrent artery of Heubner: Recurrent Artery of Heubner, a branch of the ACA, supplies the head of the caudate nucleus and the anterior limb of the internal capsule. While the recurrent artery of Heubner does supply a part of the internal capsule, its infarcts typically affect the head of the caudate and anterior limb, but it is not the most common source of strokes affecting the internal capsule overall.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The lateral striate arteries are the primary suppliers of blood to the internal capsule.
  • Due to their small size and critical location, these arteries are particularly susceptible to hypertension-induced damage, leading to lacunar strokes, which often occur in the internal capsule.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male presents with unsteady gait and slurred speech. On neurological examination, he demonstrates dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysarthria. Imaging reveals cerebellar atrophy. Dysfunction of which of the following nuclei receiving inhibitory input from Purkinje cells in the cerebellum is most likely contributing to his symptoms among given options?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Fastigial Nucleus

 

  • Purkinje cells are inhibitory to all deep cerebellar nuclei- dentate, emboliform, globose and fastigial nucleus. They also project to all vestibular nuclei.
  • Purkinje cells project inhibitory signals to the fastigial nucleus. This projection is a key part of the cerebellar circuitry that influences motor control and balance.
  • The output from the fastigial nucleus is crucial for postural adjustments and control of muscle tone, as part of the integrated motor control system.

 

OTHER OPTIONS:

 

Option A. Arcuate Nucleus: Arcuate Nucleus is a collection of neurons in the hypothalamus, involved in releasing hormones that regulate pituitary function. There is no direct connection between Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and the arcuate nucleus. The primary function of the arcuate nucleus is in the endocrine system, not in the motor control or coordination associated with cerebellar functions.

 

Option C. Superior Olivary Nucleus: Superior Olivary Nucleus is involved in auditory processing, particularly in localizing sound in the brainstem. Purkinje cells do not project directly to the superior olivary nucleus. The cerebellum and the superior olivary complex serve different functions; the former in motor control and the latter in auditory processing.

 

Option D. Ventral Lateral Thalamic Nucleus: Ventral Lateral Thalamic Nucleus is a part of the thalamus involved in motor functions. While the cerebellum does communicate with the thalamus, particularly in the context of motor coordination, Purkinje cells specifically do not project directly to the ventral lateral thalamic nucleus. Instead, the output from cerebellar nuclei (including the fastigial nucleus) reaches the thalamus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The output from the fastigial nucleus is crucial for postural adjustments and control of muscle tone, as part of the integrated motor control system.

questions.stem: Spinal accessory nerve related to which of the following triangles: Occipital triangle Subclavian triangle Muscular triangle Carotid triangle Submental triangle
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1,4

 

The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) passes through two primary triangles in the neck:

 

1. The occipital triangle, which is a part of the posterior triangle of the neck, bordered by the sternocleidomastoid muscle anteriorly, the trapezius muscle posteriorly, and the inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle inferiorly. The spinal accessory nerve travels superficially across the occipital triangle as it innervates the trapezius muscle.

 

4. The carotid triangle, which is a part of the anterior triangle of the neck, bordered by the sternocleidomastoid muscle posteriorly, the superior belly of the omohyoid muscle inferiorly, and the posterior digastric muscle superiorly. After emerging from the jugular foramen, the spinal accessory nerve crosses the carotid triangle deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which it also innervates.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 1,2: The subclavian triangle (also known as the supraclavicular or omoclavicular triangle) is not one of the primary triangles through which the spinal accessory nerve passes.

 

Option B. 2,4: While the nerve crosses the carotid triangle, it does not pass through the subclavian triangle as part of its typical anatomical route.

 

Option D. 3,5: The muscular triangle and submental triangle are not associated with the course of the spinal accessory nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The spinal accessory nerve traverses the occipital and carotid triangles of the neck.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old male was brought to ER with complaints of profuse upper GI bleed. His past history couldn’t be obtained. His BP was 60/40 and his PR 140/min. Inspite of immediate resuscitation measures initiated, the patient failed to survive. Autopsy showed a deep peptic ulcer in the lesser curvature of stomach. Which of the following arteries would have been penetrated by the ulcer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Left gastric artery

 

  • A peptic ulcer located on the lesser curvature of the stomach is most likely to penetrate the left gastric artery.
  • This artery runs along the lesser curvature and is therefore at risk of being involved by a penetrating ulcer in this location.
  • Such involvement can lead to a significant hemorrhage, as seen in this patient with profuse upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hepatic artery: The hepatic artery primarily supplies the liver and is not typically involved in ulcers on the lesser curvature of the stomach.

 

Option C. Left gastroepiploic artery: The left gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature of the stomach, making it less likely to be affected by ulcers on the lesser curvature.

 

Option D. Gastroduodenal artery: The gastroduodenal artery supplies the pylorus and the proximal duodenum and is less likely to be involved by an ulcer on the lesser curvature unless the ulcer is located at the pylorus or duodenal bulb.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The left gastric artery, which runs along the lesser curvature, is at risk of being eroded by peptic ulcers in that location, leading to potential life-threatening hemorrhages.


ore at risk of being involved by a penetrating ulcer in this location.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department with neck pain and limited range of motion following a minor car accident. Radiologic examination reveals an abnormality in the apical ligament of the dens. This ligament is embryologically derived from which of the following structures?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Notochord

 

  • The Apical Ligament of the dens, an important stabilizer of the cervical spine, is embryologically derived from the notochord.
  • In this clinical scenario, the patient's symptoms are likely related to trauma to the cervical spine, particularly involving the axis (C2) and its supporting structures.
  • The notochord gives rise to the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs and contributes to the formation of axial skeletal structures, including ligaments like the apical ligament of the dens.

 

 

 

OTHER OPTIONS:

 

Option A. Neural Tube: The neural tube is the precursor to the central nervous system, forming structures like the brain and spinal cord. While it is essential for the development of the nervous system, it does not give rise to the apical ligament of the dens.

 

Option B. Neural Crest:  Neural crest cells are a group of cells that arise from the border of the neural tube and migrate to various parts of the embryo. They contribute to the development of diverse structures, including peripheral nerves, melanocytes, and facial cartilage, but they do not form the apical ligament of the dens.

 

Option D. Neuropore: The neuropores are the openings at the ends of the neural tube during early embryonic development. The closure of the neuropores is critical in the formation of the central nervous system. The neuropores do not contribute to the development of the apical ligament of the dens.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The apical ligament of the dens is a derivative of the notochord.
  • The notochord is an embryonic structure that provides signals for the development of the vertebral column and eventually forms the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs.
  • The apical ligament of the dens represents a remnant of the notochord.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man had noticed during the past 3 months a thickening of the skin at the base of his right ring finger, which tried to pull his finger towards palm. He consulted his physician. On examination of the palms of both hands, a localized thickening of subcutaneous tissue could be felt at the base of the right ring and little fingers. The metacarpophalangeal joint of the ring finger could not be fully extended, either actively or passively. Identify the incorrect statement:

options.label: B
options.text: Palmar Aponeurosis is thickening of Deep Fascia of Palm

options.label: C
options.text: Each slip is attached to the Base of the Middle Phalanx and to the Fibrous Flexor Sheath of each finger

options.label: D
options.text: The Palmar Aponeurosis distally it divides into Four Slips

questions.answerText: Each slip is attached to the Base of the Middle Phalanx and to the Fibrous Flexor Sheath of each finger
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Each slip is attached to the Base of the Middle Phalanx and to the Fibrous Flexor Sheath of each finger

 

The palmar aponeurosis is thickening of the deep fascia of the palm. It is attached to the base of the proximal phalanx and fibrous flexor sheath of each finger.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The patient had Dupuytren's Contracture: Dupuytren's Contracture is characterized by progressive thickening and shortening of the palmar fascia, leading to flexion contractures of the fingers, commonly the ring and little fingers.

 

 

The symptoms described, including the thickening of the skin at the base of the ring finger and the inability to fully extend the metacarpophalangeal joint, align with Dupuytren's contracture.

 

Option B. Palmar Aponeurosis is thickening of Deep Fascia of Palm: The palmar aponeurosis is indeed a thickening of the deep fascia in the palm of the hand. It plays a key role in the structure and function of the hand, and its pathological thickening and contraction are central to Dupuytren's contracture.

 

Option D. The Palmar Aponeurosis distally it divides into Four Slips: The palmar aponeurosis distally divides into slips that extend towards the fingers. While the number of slips can vary, typically, it divides into four or five slips extending towards the digits.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Each Slip is Attached to the Base of the Middle Phalanx and to the Fibrous Flexor Sheath of Each Finger: 
  • In Dupuytren's contracture, the pathological changes occur in the palmar aponeurosis and related structures.
  • However, the palmar aponeurosis does not normally attach to the base of the middle phalanx. Instead, it primarily attaches to the bases of the proximal phalanges and the overlying skin.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old female, manual labourer at a construction site, accidentally stepped over a sharp-edged blade in the site, following which there was severe bleeding from her sole. She was taken to a nearby hospital, where with much difficulty, the bleeding was arrested and cut ends were sutured. Which of the following statements pertaining to the above case is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Blood supply to sole is from branches of posterior tibial artery

options.label: B
options.text: Lateral plantar artery is the larger terminal branch and forms the plantar arterial arch

options.label: C
options.text: Plantar arterial arch will give rise to four plantar metatarsal arteries

options.label: D
options.text: Plantar arterial arch lies between the second & third layer of sole

questions.answerText: Plantar arterial arch lies between the second & third layer of sole
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Plantar arterial arch lies between the second & third layer of sole

 

  • The trunks of neurovascular bundles lie between the first & second layer of the sole.
  • In the context of a severe foot injury involving significant bleeding in the sole, understanding the vascular anatomy of the foot is crucial.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blood supply to sole is from branches of posterior tibial artery: The sole of the foot primarily receives its blood supply from branches of the posterior tibial artery. The posterior tibial artery, after passing posterior to the medial malleolus, enters the sole of the foot where it divides into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.

 

Option B. Lateral plantar artery is the larger terminal branch and forms the plantar arterial arch: The lateral plantar artery, a terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery, is indeed the larger of the two terminal branches. It curves medially on the sole of the foot, forming the plantar arterial arch. This arch plays a critical role in supplying blood to the plantar surface of the foot.

 

Option C. Plantar arterial arch will give rise to four plantar metatarsal arteries: The plantar arterial arch typically gives rise to four plantar metatarsal arteries. These arteries further divide into digital branches to supply the toes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The plantar arterial arch lies deep to the tendons of the flexor digitorum brevis, which is in the second layer of the sole. It does not lie between the second and third layers but rather deep to the second layer.

questions.stem: A student after a heavy lunch from the hostel got ready for his afternoon class. After a while he yawned widely. To his surprise sadly he could not close his mouth. The jaw was stuck. Which of the following statement is not true in the above scenario?

options.label: A
options.text: This is a case of anterior dislocation of temporomandibular joint

options.label: B
options.text: Temporomandibular joint is a bicondylar type of synovial joint

options.label: C
options.text: Contraction of medial pterygoid depresses the mandible

options.label: D
options.text: Sphenomandibular ligament is situated medial to temporomandibular joint

questions.answerText: Contraction of medial pterygoid depresses the mandible
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Contraction of medial pterygoid depresses the mandible

 

  • The medial pterygoid muscle, along with the lateral pterygoid, masseter, and temporalis muscles, is one of the muscles of mastication.
  • The primary action of the medial pterygoid muscle is elevation of the mandible, not depression.
  • The depression of the mandible, or opening the mouth, is primarily accomplished by the lateral pterygoid muscle and the suprahyoid muscles, especially when the mouth is opened wide, as in a yawn.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. This is a case of anterior dislocation of temporomandibular joint: This is likely true given the scenario where the student is unable to close his mouth after a wide yawn, which can cause an anterior dislocation of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ).

 

Option B. Temporomandibular joint is a bicondylar type of synovial joint: This is true. The TMJ is a type of synovial joint that involves the condyle of the mandible and the articular fossa of the temporal bone.

 

Option D. Sphenomandibular ligament is situated medial to temporomandibular joint: This is also true. The sphenomandibular ligament is one of the ligaments of the TMJ located medially to the joint.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The medial pterygoid muscle functions to elevate the mandible, not depress it. In the context of a TMJ dislocation, which often occurs with an anterior dislocation after activities such as yawning, the inability to close the mouth is a key clinical sign.
  • Understanding the anatomy and function of the muscles of mastication and the ligaments of the TMJ is important for diagnosing and managing TMJ disorders.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following features are seen by the lesion of the marked structure in the given image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans: D) Contralateral Hemiplegia

 

  • Marked structure is a pyramid on the ventral surface of medulla just lateral to anterior median fissure.
  • The corticospinal fibres lie underneath the pyramid. Lesion of which will cause contralateral hemiplegia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ataxia: Ataxia refers to a lack of muscle coordination that can affect speech, eye movements, the ability to swallow, walking, and other voluntary movements. It is commonly associated with lesions in the cerebellum or in the sensory pathways.

 

Option B. Vertigo: Vertigo is a sense of spinning or dizziness, often related to problems in the inner ear or vestibular system. Lesions in the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem, the vestibulocochlear nerve, or the inner ear can lead to vertigo.

 

Option C. Ipsilateral Facial Nerve Palsy: Ipsilateral Facial Nerve Palsy refers to weakness or paralysis of the facial muscles on the same side as the lesion. It is commonly associated with lesions affecting the facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII), which could be at the level of the brainstem or the nerve itself.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Contralateral Hemiplegia:  This is paralysis on the side of the body opposite to the side of the brain where the lesion is located.
  • Lesions in the motor pathways, especially in the cerebral cortex or internal capsule, can lead to contralateral hemiplegia because motor fibers decussate (cross over) in the medulla.


ers to a lack of muscle coordination that can affect speech, eye movements, the ability to swallow, walking, and other voluntary movements. It is commonly associated with lesions in the cerebellum or in the sensory pathways.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with difficulty in finger movements, specifically in extending his fingers. During a detailed musculoskeletal examination, you assess the involvement of various muscles in the dorsal digital expansion. Which of the following muscles does not participate in the dorsal digital expansion?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Adductor Pollicis

 

  • The dorsal digital expansion (extensor hood) is a complex structure that allows for coordinated finger movements. It is primarily formed by the tendons of the extensor digitorum, lumbricals, and interossei muscles.
  •  These muscles work together to extend the fingers at the interphalangeal joints and flex at the metacarpophalangeal joints.
  • The adductor pollicis, however, is a muscle of the thumb that does not contribute to the dorsal digital expansion. It is responsible for adducting the thumb and does not play a role in finger extension.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Extensor Digitorum: This muscle inserts into the dorsal digital expansion and is crucial for extending the fingers.

 

Option B. Lumbricals: These muscles attach to the extensor hoods and assist in extending the fingers at the interphalangeal joints while flexing the metacarpophalangeal joints.

 

Option C. Interossei: These muscles also attach to the extensor hoods and play a role in both finger abduction/adduction and extension at the interphalangeal joints.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The adductor pollicis does not participate in the dorsal digital expansion, which is primarily involved in finger extension and is formed by the extensor digitorum, lumbricals, and interossei muscles.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old basketball player sprained his right ankle after landing on an opponent's foot following a jump shot. His ankle inverted, causing severe pain and rapid swelling. He could not bear weight on the injured ankle. An X-ray showed no evidence of fractures in the lower limb bones. This is his first ankle injury. Which structure related to the ankle joint is most likely injured in this case?

options.label: D
options.text: Tibio Talar part of Deltoid Ligament

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anterior Talo-Fibular Ligament

 

  • The most common ligament injured in an ankle sprain, particularly with an inversion mechanism (where the ankle rolls outward), is the Anterior Talo-Fibular Ligament (ATFL).
  • The ATFL is part of the lateral ligament complex of the ankle and is the weakest and most frequently injured ligament during such events.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Tibio-Calcaneal part of Deltoid Ligament: This ligament is part of the medial ligament complex (deltoid ligament) and is less commonly injured in inversion sprains.

 

Option C. Capsular Ligament: This term is less specific and does not typically refer to a primary structure injured in an ankle sprain.

 

Option D. Tibio Talar part of Deltoid Ligament: This is another part of the deltoid ligament on the medial side of the ankle, which is not typically involved in inversion injuries.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The Anterior Talo-Fibular Ligament (ATFL) is the most commonly injured ligament in ankle sprains, especially when the injury mechanism involves inversion of the foot.



er to a primary structure injured in an ankle sprain.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient is scheduled for central venous catheter placement. The anesthesiologist discusses the landmarks used to identify the internal jugular vein for cannulation. Which of the following surface landmarks is used for this purpose?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Sedillot’s triangle

 

  • Sedillot’s triangle, also known as the lesser supraclavicular fossa, is an anatomical landmark used to locate the internal jugular vein for cannulation.
  • It is bounded by the clavicle inferiorly, the sternal head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle medially, and the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle laterally.
  • This triangle is used as a guide to access the internal jugular vein because it provides a relatively superficial and direct route to the vein.

 

 

Stemocleidomastoid muscle: SM: stemal head; CM: Cleidal head

 

Red dot: triangle of sedillot CL: clavicle

 

Triangle of Sedillot:

 

  • Medially -sternal head of sternocleidomastoid
  • Laterally-clavicular head of sternocleidomastoid
  • Base-Clavicle
  • Content -Internal jugular vein.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Subclavian triangle: This is not the primary landmark for internal jugular vein cannulation. It is more relevant for accessing the subclavian vein.

 

Option C. Scaleno Vertebral triangle: This is not typically used for venous cannulation but rather for identifying structures in the neck related to the scalene muscles and vertebrae.

 

Option D. Suboccipital triangle: This triangle is located at the posterior aspect of the neck and is not relevant for internal jugular vein cannulation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Sedillot’s triangle (lesser supraclavicular fossa) is the surface landmark used for cannulating the internal jugular vein, providing a direct and superficial route for venous access.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old male, chronic smoker, visited his physician with complaints of persistent cough, weight loss, and for the past few days, there was blood in his sputum. He also noticed an absence of sweating on the right side of his face. On examination, partial ptosis and constriction of the pupil were noted in the right eye. A PA view of a chest X-ray showed a lesion in the apex of the right lung. Which of the following structures does not form a posterior relation to the apex of the lung?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Middle Trunk of Brachial Plexus

 

  • The Middle Trunk of the Brachial Plexus originates from the C7 nerve root and lies more laterally and anteriorly, not forming a posterior relation to the apex of the lung.

 

Posterior relations of apex of the lung

 

• Neck of the 1st rib.

• Structures between apex & neck of 1st rib.

• From medial to lateral

1. Sympathetic chain (cervicothoracic ganglion)

2. Supreme intercostal vein

3. Superior intercostal artery

4. Ventral ramus of 1st thoracic nerve

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Highest Intercostal Vein: This structure is a posterior relation to the apex of the lung and drains into the brachiocephalic vein and is located posteriorly.

 

Option C. Sympathetic Chain:  This structure is a posterior relation to the apex of the lung and runs alongside of the vertebral column

 

Option D. Ventral Ramus of T1:  This structure is a posterior relation to the apex of the lung and exits the spinal cord thus contributing to the brachial plexus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The middle trunk of the brachial plexus does not form a posterior relation to the apex of the lung, whereas the highest intercostal vein, sympathetic chain, and ventral ramus of T1 do.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents with chronic abdominal pain. During an exploratory laparotomy, a large nerve ganglion is noted in the mesentery. Histological examination reveals neurons with large cell bodies and a large, eccentric nucleus. Which of the following is the most likely location of these neurons?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Spinal ganglia

 

  • Spinal ganglia, also known as dorsal root ganglia, contain neurons with large cell bodies and a large, eccentric nucleus.
  • These characteristics are typical of the ganglia found in the spinal ganglia, which are responsible for transmitting sensory information from the periphery to the central nervous system.

 

 

Other Options

 

Option B. Ganglia in mesenteric plexus: Ganglia in the mesenteric plexus, also known as the enteric nervous system, contain neurons that typically have centrally located nuclei. The description of neurons with large, eccentric nuclei does not match the typical histological appearance of the mesenteric plexus ganglia.

 

Option C. Coeliac ganglia: The coeliac ganglia, part of the sympathetic nervous system, also contain neurons, but these neurons do not typically have large, eccentric nuclei. These ganglia are involved in the autonomic innervation of abdominal organs but have a different histological appearance.

 

Option D. Cervical ganglia: Cervical ganglia are part of the sympathetic chain in the neck. Neurons in these ganglia do not typically have the described large, eccentric nuclei. They are involved in the sympathetic innervation of the head, neck, and upper limbs.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Neurons in the spinal ganglia are characterized by large cell bodies and large, eccentric nuclei, which are distinguishing features of these sensory ganglia.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement is incorrect regarding the anatomical structure known as Sibson's fascia?

options.label: A
options.text: Covers the apical part of the lung

options.label: D
options.text: Attached to the inner border of the 2nd rib

questions.answerText: Attached to the inner border of the 2nd rib
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Attached to the inner border of the 2nd rib

 

  • Sibson's fascia, also known as the suprapleural membrane, is an anatomical structure that extends over the apex of the lung.
  • It serves as a protective layer and provides support to the thoracic inlet. This fascia is not attached to the inner border of the 2nd rib.
  • Instead, it attaches to the inner border of the first rib and the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Covers the apical part of the lung: This is correct because Sibson's fascia indeed covers the apex of the lung, providing an additional protective layer.

 

Option B. Vessels pass above the fascia: This is correct as the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus pass above Sibson's fascia, highlighting its protective role.

 

Option C. Part of scalenus minimus muscle: This is correct because Sibson's fascia is sometimes considered to be a thickened extension of the endothoracic fascia, and it is associated with the scalenus minimus muscle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Sibson's fascia, or the suprapleural membrane, is attached to the inner border of the first rib and the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra, not the second rib.

questions.stem: A 42-year old male is diagnosed with a tumor located in the uncinate process of the pancreas. Which of the following vessels is most likely to be affected by a tumor in the uncinate process of the pancreas?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior mesenteric artery

 

  • The uncinate process of the pancreas is a projection that extends posteriorly and to the left from the lower part of the head of the pancreas, lying posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
  • A tumor in the uncinate process is most likely to affect the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) due to its close anatomical relationship.
  • The SMA supplies blood to the intestines, and its compression can lead to significant clinical symptoms related to intestinal ischemia.

 

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Portal vein: The portal vein is formed by the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein, and it lies more posteriorly to the pancreas. While a large tumor in the head of the pancreas might affect the portal vein, the uncinate process specifically is more closely associated with the superior mesenteric artery.

 

Option C. Common hepatic artery: The common hepatic artery arises from the celiac trunk and courses towards the liver, but it is not typically affected by tumors in the uncinate process due to its anatomical position.

 

Option D. Inferior mesenteric artery: The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the abdominal aorta and supplies the distal part of the colon. It is anatomically distant from the uncinate process of the pancreas and unlikely to be affected by a tumor in this location.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • A tumor in the uncinate process of the pancreas is most likely to affect the superior mesenteric artery due to its close anatomical relationship.
